1
PGS principles, policies and procedures
I. Membership procedure
On application every prospective farmer/producer member of the Outeniqua PGS will do the
following:
1. Sign the farmer member pledge.
2. Certain groups or individuals may be unable to read and sign the documentation. If this is
the case, the following procedure will apply:
All procedures will be explained to the group/individual.
● The group/individual will be required to make a verbal pledge or commitment to
the code of conduct and procedures of the PGS.
● This pledge will be recorded by the PGS through photographic or other
documented record.
● Documentation will be completed by the PGS administrator on behalf of the
group/individual with his/their consent as recorded.
1. Supply the Outeniqua PGS with all relevant information to facilitate assessment.
2. Familiarise themselves with the Basic Production Principles and the SAOSO Standard for
Organic Production and Processing.
3. Familiarise themselves with all guidelines, documentation and procedures of our PGS.
II. Membership fees, farm assessment fees, licensing fees
2.1 Membership Fees
● Outeniqua Natural and Organic PGS membership fees: At our annual AGM held in 2025,
our PGS group members approved the following fees:
o Annual Farmer & consumer Membership fee: R 100
● PGS South Africa membership fee: the group will pay the annual membership fee to
SAOSO. The funds for this national membership will be secured from our membership
fees set out in 1.
o Currently R500
2
2.2PGS farm assessment and certification fee
The PGS farm assessment and certification fee covers administrative coordination,
preparation, facilitation of the farm visit, reporting, peer review processes and certification
decision-making carried out by the PGS administrator. The fee is designed on a cost-recovery
basis and reflects the scale and commercial intensity of the farming operation.
2.3PGS assessment fee structure (initial certification and renewal)
The farm assessment visit fee is set based on a sliding scale (see below), excluding transport
costs for the administrator (charged at an AA rate per km). This fee applies to all commercial
farms entering or renewing PGS certification. The assessment fee increases progressively
with annual farm turnover to reflect increased operational complexity, production volume
and market exposure.
Annual farm turnover (gross sales) Initial certification fee (R) Renewal fee (R)
Below R 250,000 1,500 900
R 250,001 – R 500,000 2,500 2,000
R 500,001 – R 1,000,000 3,000 2,500
R 1,000,001 – R 2,500,000 3,700 3,200
R 2,500,001 – R 5,000,000 5,000 5,000
Above R 5,000,000 8,000 8,000
● Fees are per farm assessment visit.
● Transport costs for the PGS administrator are charged separately at cost. (AA rate)
Where possible, farm visits may be clustered geographically to reduce transport
expenses.
● Members of the assessment team will carry their own cost of transport if they cannot
travel with the administrator.
● Renewal fees apply only where no significant changes to land, production system,
or inputs have occurred.
● Where major changes are identified, the PGS group may require a full assessment
at the initial certification rate.
● Annual turnover is self-declared by the farmer and subject to peer review within
the PGS group.
● Fees are payable prior to the farm assessment visit.
● Only fully paid-up members will be eligible for farm assessments and receive
certificates.
3
2.4Farm visit fee payable by participants
● In the event that the farmer is happy to offer some catering, for each PGS farm
visit, the following contributions apply to cover basic catering costs:
o Non-members contribute R50 per visit, inclusive of snacks.
o Members contribute R30 per visit toward catering. The R30 member
contribution is paid to the host farmer to offset catering costs. Any
remaining amount, where applicable, is allocated to the PGS fund.
● No fee will be applicable to members if no catering is offered, in which case farm visit
participants can be asked to bring their own snack.
2.5 Fee for the use of seal
Once the farm is certified, the farmer will receive the high-resolution seal(s) to be used for labelling
purposes. The farmer is to carry all printing costs. The licensing fee is R500 per annum per farm.
And shall be paid to the PGS fund, which will then pay this over to SAOSO. The farmer is not
authorized to share the seal with any other party and the PGS administrating team is the custodian
of the good use of the PGS seal.
III. PGS committee and meetings
3.1PGS core Committee election and composition
● Members will elect a committee to plan and implement the work of our PGS for the
year and review farm assessments.
● The composition of the committee is to be renewed at each AGM.
● Farmers to represent no less than 50% of the committee.

3.2Frequency of meetings
● Members will be invited to take part in quarterly meetings to discuss the activities of
the Outeniqua PGS, share knowledge, assist one another with any production issues
and share and exchange seeds.
● Members are required to attend our annual group meeting.
● All farmers are to attend at least two other farm visits annually.
3.3Composition of the farm visit Committee
● Farm visits committees will be composed of a minimum of 4 people (administrator, 1
consumer and 2 farmers) – the visited farm can also indicate a maximum number of
additional participants who will attend the visit as observers and who shall not disrupt
the assessment process.
● Independent retailer/market members (or their representatives) are expected to
attend all farm visits from where they source organic produce.
● Failure to comply with 2 and 6 will lead to action laid out in the consequences for non-
compliance section of this document.
● Farm visits are open to all members and non-members.
IV. Assessment Process:
4.1 Preparation for the assessment:
1. After a written application, the applicant will be given at least 5 days’ notice before the
assessment date.
5
2. The assessment questionnaire must reach assessment team members 3 days prior to
assessment in order for all members to study the document. The assessment team must
consist of at least the following:
● One committee member responsible for the administration of the visit.
● A minimum of two “peer members”– a “peer member” is a farmer/producer who is a
member of a PGS and has knowledge or understanding of the production on the
farm/production being assessed.
● One “public” member – a customer or independent retailer who would normally consume
and/or purchase the product/s from the assessed farm.
● Should none of the group members hold the specific knowledge required for a farm visited,
a technical expert should be included in the group.
3. Once the administrator has received all the above documentation, it will be forwarded to
members of the assessment team.
4.2Assessment:
1) The committee member responsible for the administration of the farm visit will be
responsible for completing the assessment report and will “drive” the process.
2) All participants on the farm visit will complete the “Farm visit checklist”
3) All members have the right to ask questions and can explore any query that might have
arisen out of the supplied documentation prior to the assessment.
4) A walkthrough of the farm/production premises will be conducted and Q&A will take place
during this walkthrough.
5) After the walkthrough, all comments, suggestions or further queries will be handled in a
short meeting before discussing the assessment. This meeting is an open forum. All
participants will be expected to give their comments openly at this meeting. A
prospective applicant has the right to hear these comments first hand and will be given
the opportunity to respond to or clarify any misunderstanding. The aim is to limit further
off-premises or long-distance discussion to the absolute minimum. Ideally, the
assessment process should be finalised up to the provisional acceptance stage at that
meeting. But in some instances, when the members are not able to come to a
conclusion, further investigation may be required. This should be completed and
members of the visiting committee should come to conclusion on the assessment no
later than 5 days after the farm visit.
6) Results will be collated, further verification conducted (if necessary) and actions and/or
remedies requested.
7) Timelines for all the above must be recorded.
8) As soon as the applicant has complied with these requests, all results will be collated and
a final report completed/submitted.
9) Farmer members who have taken part in the visit will be asked to share insights and scope
for improving practices in a peer review analysis to be collated to the final report.
10) The committee will review the approval documentation at their quarterly meetings
11) All documentation regarding the assessment will be filed and administered by the
Outeniqua PGS administrator.
12) Traceability: Retailer and market members or farmer members selling their own produce
shall ensure that an invoicing/delivery note system is in place to ensure an audit trail from
farm to marketplace. This must be accessible to the committee as part of quality
management and be available for the resolution of queries or complaints.
6
4.3Follow-up Assessments:
All producers will be assessed annually, based on the same procedure and notice period.
4.4Random or unannounced assessments:
The Outeniqua PGS reserves the right to do random or unannounced visits to production premises
under the following circumstances:
. If a complaint IN WRITING is received regarding the product of any
farmer/producer, an unannounced visit may be scheduled. (see section on
dealing with non-compliance)
. A number of random visits can be undertaken to members prior to annual
assessments as part of quality management.
4.5Non-compliance and discipline:
PGS is at its most effective when all members are operating according to its rules and in the spirit
of organic principles. The first action to be taken in any case of ill-discipline or transgression is the
path of informal counselling, mentoring and practical assistance prior to any official action. It needs
to be understood that all members should conduct themselves according to the signed pledge and
comply with the Standard Operating Procedures and produce their goods in compliance with the
Basic Production Principles. If there is any reason to believe that any member is operating or
conducting him/herself outside the stated guidelines and the first action (if applicable), of inter-
member guidance or counselling is ineffective, formal action may be instituted.
This will be done according to the following guidelines:
1. Only complaints received in writing will be attended to. Our PGS cannot react to random
or unfounded verbal complaints or allegations.
2. Type of complaint:
a. If the complaint is regarding unacceptable production or farming practices, a
visit to the production premises will precede a complaint hearing. This visit
may be unannounced, and must include at least the administrator, a
committee member and one other unaffected member of our PGS. During this
visit, the same procedures will be followed as with a scheduled assessment,
with specific focus on the nature of the complaint. After the visit, the
procedures as described below will be followed.
b. If the complaint is regarding member conduct only, (a.) above will be deemed
unnecessary and procedure (c.) will be followed.
c. A minuted meeting will be called with the following persons present:
1. The member against whom the complaint is levelled
2. The administrator of the Outeniqua PGS
3. A committee member of the Outeniqua PGS
● At least one additional group member or PGSSA member not involved in the
complaint.
● A person deemed competent to record the proceedings.
7
● The complainant or authorised representative. If this is not possible, [the
complainant will be expected to produce a written account of the complaint; in
such case, the complainant shall accept the outcome of the ruling.
4. The complaint will be read to the member, and physical or documented proof and/or
evidence will be presented. The member will have an opportunity to answer or explain
his/her actions, and supply evidence or proof to substantiate his/her reply. If deemed
necessary, the complainant may be present or be called for his/her response.
5. The meeting will rule on the validity of the complaint, after hearing both parties’
submissions and may rule as follows:
a. Rejection of complaint: If the complaint is deemed invalid, both parties will be
informed and the decision recorded. The decision will be communicated in
writing to affected parties.
b. Acceptance of complaint: If the complaint is justified, action will be taken against
the concerned member; the meeting will assess the level of misconduct,
implement the appropriate action, and communicate the decision in writing to
affected parties.
Action:
● First warning: If this is the first time a member has transgressed a non-critical
requirement, the member will receive a first warning. The warning will be active for
one calendar year. Any action not described below in para. (c.) is deemed a non-
critical transgression.
● Second warning: A second warning for a similar transgression during one calendar
year will result in cancellation of membership.
● Serious misconduct: If the transgression is deemed to be serious misconduct,
membership will be terminated immediately without a warning.
Examples of serious misconduct are:
● Public abuse (physical or otherwise) of fellow PGS members and/or customers.
● Any action that brings the PGS into disrepute.
● The use or application of any substance or additive specifically prohibited by the
SAOSO Standard for Organic Production and Processing or by the Basic Production
Principles. For example, any production practices that could impact on the organic
nature of the end product, i.e. the addition of unacceptable inputs, intentional use of
GMOs, contamination of the product with pollutants, chemicals etc.
● The failure to implement corrective actions marked as critical as required during a
PGS assessment visit.
● Any criminal action as described in the Statutes and Laws of the Republic of South
Africa.
● The sale of any un-assessed product bearing our PGS endorsement logo or otherwise
marketed as a PGS endorsed product.
● The sale of any product bearing the logo or registration number of a third-party
certifier, or otherwise marketed as organic, and found not to be compliant with the
requirements of the certifying body. Such a transgression will also be reported to the
relevant certifier.
Termination of membership will be seen as a last resort. The committee is required to take into
account mitigating circumstances.
8
4.6 Termination of membership:
● If membership is terminated due to a critical transgression, the right to market their
products bearing our endorsement and logo will be forfeited.
● If the membership is terminated due to a non-critical transgression, membership and the
right to use our logo will not be revoked, but the member will be under probation for one
calendar year following the ruling.
4.7 Reinstatement of membership:
Any member whose membership was terminated due to a non-critical transgression, may, after
one calendar year from the termination, re-apply for membership. All previous transgressions
will be deemed nullified and the application will be assessed and treated like a new application.

national working group

forthcoming.
VI. Aggregation of produce within the PGS
6.1 Principles governing aggregation
Where a Outeniqua PGS-certified farm aggregates produce (i.e buys in ) from more than one
source, each case of aggregation must be assessed and approved by the PGS group on a
case-by-case basis, in accordance with Participatory Guarantee System principles of
transparency, trust and collective responsibility.
The following minimum criteria apply:
● Participation and commitment to the PGS process.
● The aggregating farm/entity must demonstrate active participation in PGS
meetings, peer reviews and farm assessments, confirming commitment to the
principles and functioning of the PGS system.
10
● The aggregating farm/entity must show evidence of its commitment to organic
agriculture through its own PGS assessment and compliance history.
6.2 Commitments and declarations from supplying farms
Each supplying farm must provide a signed declaration confirming that:
● No prohibited synthetic chemicals are used in their production.
● Production is undertaken with the intention of meeting organic standards.
● The farm commits to progressing towards organic certification and PGS certification
within 6 months.
6.3 Traceability and documentation
Full traceability must be ensured for all aggregated produce. Invoices and delivery notes
must clearly indicate:
● The name of each supplying farm.
● The certification or PGS status of each supplying farm.
● Produce quantities and line items linked to each supplying farm.
6.4 Aggregation involving non-organic (conventional) farms
Where produce from non-organic farms is aggregated, the following minimum safeguards
apply:
● Physical separation of organic and non-organic produce during harvesting, packing,
storage, transport, and delivery.
● A signed declaration from the aggregating farm confirming that separation
procedures are implemented and monitored
● Invoices and records must be clearly itemised to distinguish organic and non-organic
produce.
In line with the developmental nature of PGS, such farms should be encouraged to convert to
organic agriculture and be introduced to the PGS network.
11
6.5Labelling requirements for aggregated produce
In order to avoid misleading consumers, where aggregation from different production
systems occurs, each product batch sold by a farmer, retailer, or marketplace must be clearly
identified according to its method of production.
Above the afore-mentioned labels, the following additional labelling categories apply in retail
and market settings:
Self-claim
organic
Applies where there is no organic
certification and the organic claim is self-
declared.
The farmer must use their own
label or seal.
No PGS claims may be made.
In an aggregated set-up, the
self-claim can only be allowed
for 6 months after which a PGS
assessment will be required
from the date of notification.
Conventional Applies where production is not organic. The farmer must use their own
label or seal.
No organic or PGS claims may be
made.
Free range Applies to animals and eggs produced by
poultry that:
- have outdoor access, as defined under
the South African regulations for free-
range production,
- but are not necessarily pasture-based
systems.
- are not under organic management
practices
The farmer must use their own
label or seal.
No PGS claims may be made.

FARMER PLEDGE
I/We: ____________________________________________ (Farmer/Farmer Group Name) hereby solemnly
declare and affirm that
□ I/We support and actively pursue the principles of organic agriculture as described by IFOAM-Organics
International and the Basic Production Principles, and that these principles were explained to us.
I/we further declare that:
● I/We will submit correct and accurate information about my/our production unit, and that I/we
will keep all information current, complete and up to date to reflect any changes.
● I/We have read and understood the Basic Production Principles and our growing methods adhere
to the requirements listed therein.
● I/We understand that our PGS group reserves the right to remove us from the program and deny
us the use of the logo and marketing materials for any reason including concerns that we have
violated listed growing practices, or have missing or misleading information on the application.
● I/We will only represent products as organically grown when they actually meet the assessment
standards and were produced on land that has been endorsed by the Outeniqua PGS.
● All the land for which I/we are applying for PGS endorsement has been free of prohibited
pesticides, herbicides and fertilisers for at least 12 months before sowing or planting in the case of
annual production; 12 months before grazing or harvest for pastures and meadows and/or 18
months before harvest for other perennials from the date of our first harvest this year.
OR
□ I/We have applied for In-Conversion status (select which case applies to your farm or PGS group)
● I/We do not use any prohibited pesticides, herbicides or fertilisers now, but we are still
within the □ 12 months or □ 18 months (select) in-conversion period.
● I/We are practising agriculture without the use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides, but
we are still developing our comprehensive organic management system, and plan to
implement the changes to our practices as recommended by the Outeniqua PGS.

CONSUMER PLEDGE
I____________________________________________ hereby solemnly declare and affirm that I
support and actively pursue the principles of organic agriculture as described by the International
Federation of Organic Agriculture Movements (IFOAM-Organics International) and the Basic
Production Principles.
The IFOAM-Organics International definition:
“Organic agriculture is a production system that sustains the health of soils, ecosystems and people. It
relies on ecological processes, biodiversity and cycles adapted to local conditions, rather than the use
of inputs with adverse effects. Organic agriculture combines tradition, innovation and science to
benefit the shared environment and promote fair relationships and a good quality of life for all
involved.”
1. Principle of health: Organic Agriculture should sustain and enhance the health of soil, plant,
animal, human and planet as one and indivisible.
1. Principle of ecology: Organic Agriculture should be based on living ecological systems and
cycles, work with them, emulate them and help sustain them.
1. Principle of fairness: Organic Agriculture should build on relationships that ensure fairness
with regard to the common environment and life opportunities
1. Principle of care: Organic Agriculture should be managed in a precautionary and responsible
manner to protect the health and well-being of current and future generations and the
environment.
I agree to abide by the processes described in the PGS documentation and to support the Outeniqua
PGS.
